title: Demographic drivers of population growth among four populations of imperiled bird species
content:
Abstract
An understanding of the factors driving animal populations requires knowledge of demographic changes that underlie associated changes in population size or growth rates. Describing demographic variation in wild populations is often difficult given that some demographic rates are consistently hard to measure with sufficient precision, and long-term studies are generally needed to provide sample sizes that account for temporal variation. To provide greater insight into variation in demographic drivers among bird populations, we leveraged long-term datasets to investigate contributors of population growth for 4 populations of threatened and endangered species (Aphelocoma coerulescens [Florida Scrub-Jay], Dryobates borealis [Red-cockaded Woodpecker], and 2 populations of Ammodramus savannarum floridanus [Florida Grasshopper Sparrow]) in the Avon Park Air Force Range Sentinel Landscape in south-central Florida, USA. More specifically, we examined the relative contribution of 3 primary demographic rates—adult survival (proxy for number of deaths), recruitment (proxy for number of births), and immigration—to population growth (λ) in the 4 populations using a life table response experiment (LTRE) framework. Demographic drivers (sensitivities) varied among the 4 populations, with adult survival and immigration (about equal) having the largest contribution to growth in the first A. s. floridanus population, immigration having the greatest contribution to growth in the second A. s. floridanus population, adult survival and recruitment having the largest contributions to growth in A. coerulescens, and recruitment having the greatest contribution to growth in the D. borealis. Our findings demonstrate how demographic drivers can vary among bird species inhabiting the same conservation area and region, where similar management strategies may be used, and emphasize the role of juvenile survival for avian population dynamics. Our findings also highlight the potential need for land managers to consider the demographics of species separately when developing management and recovery guidelines for avian communities.
